titel: FIFO, securities account transfers and tax deferral
kurz: Which units count as sold in a partial sale, what happens for tax purposes on a securities account transfer or a gift, and what advantage deferring tax until the sale brings.

bloecke.md:
Besides its market value, every portfolio contains a second figure that appears on no statement: the **latent tax**. Of every unrealised price gain on individual shares, only around 73.6% economically belongs to the investor, or around 81.5% for an equity ETF because of the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung). The rest belongs to the tax office, but it only falls due on sale.

Unlike with property, since 2009 there has no longer been a holding period for securities after which gains become tax-free. The ten-year period under Section 23 EStG (Income Tax Act) applies to land and buildings, but not to shares and fund units. A long holding period therefore does not make a gain on securities tax-free; it only postpones the point at which the tax falls due. All the room for tax planning rests on this postponement. There are three starting points: the order in which units are sold, the place where the units are held, and the timing of realisation.

## Order of sale under the FIFO principle

For fungible securities held in collective safe custody (Sammelverwahrung), the law assumes that the units acquired first were sold first (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG). This rule is called FIFO, short for “first in, first out”. It is a statutory fiction that cannot be rebutted by evidence. An instruction to the bank such as “please sell the expensive units from 2024” is irrelevant for tax purposes. FIFO applies separately to each securities account and each security. All that counts is what is held in that one securities account under the same ISIN.

For a savings plan that has flowed into the same ETF over years, this has an unfavourable consequence. The oldest units are as a rule the cheapest and contain the largest book gain. Even a small partial withdrawal therefore draws on the units whose sale costs the most tax.

An equity ETF with a 30% partial exemption was bought three times, 100 units each time. The price today is €160, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) has been used up, and no church tax is due.

- 100 units at €50 (2014) = €5,000
- 100 units at €90 (2019) = €9,000
- 100 units at €130 (2024) = €13,000

The investor sells 100 units for €16,000.

Under FIFO, the 2014 tranche counts as sold. The gain is €11,000, of which €7,700 is taxable after the partial exemption. The tax is 7,700 × 26.375% = €2,030.875, or €2,030.87 after rounding the solidarity surcharge down to whole cents.

If the 2024 tranche could be chosen, the gain would be €3,000, €2,100 would be taxable and the tax would be €553.87.

With the same sale proceeds, the difference is €1,477. If €16,000 is needed net rather than gross, around 114 units instead of 100 have to be sold under FIFO.

bloecke.unter: Each tranche is worth €16,000 today, but the book gain it contains ranges from €3,000 to €11,000. Under FIFO, the tranche on the left is sold first.

bloecke.md:
## Separate securities accounts

Because FIFO applies separately to each securities account, the order can only be influenced legally by spreading the holdings across different securities accounts. An investor who builds up the long-term core holding through a savings plan in securities account A and places later, more expensive purchases in account B can later decide which account to sell from. Account B can also be a second securities account or sub-account at the same bank, because, according to the circular of the Federal Ministry of Finance (BMF) of 14 May 2025 (paras. 97 and 98), FIFO applies separately to each securities account there too. The exemption order and loss offsetting then continue to cover both accounts. If account B is held at another bank, this creates additional administrative work. The exemption order then has to be split between the two institutions, and losses at one bank are not automatically offset against gains at the other.

The separation must exist from the start. As soon as old and new units of the same ISIN are held in one securities account, it is no longer possible to choose a tranche. A later partial transfer does not reliably help, because it is not the customer who decides which units are transferred.

Separation is particularly useful for genuine old holdings. Price gains on individual shares bought before 1 January 2009 are still tax-free today (transitional rule in Section 52(28) EStG). If such units are held in the same securities account as later purchases of the same share, they are sold first under FIFO. That sale is tax-free, but the tax exemption is then used up for good. For fund units, the investment tax reform limited this grandfathering as of 31 December 2017 in any case. Only the increases in value accrued up to then remain tax-free there. For the period after that, there is a personal allowance of €100,000 under Section 56(6) InvStG (Investment Tax Act), which only takes effect through the tax return.
The FIFO rule is mandatory. Only the structure of the securities accounts can be arranged, and this only works if it is set up before the purchase.

## Securities account transfer with and without a change of creditor

Changing banks has no tax consequences as long as the owner remains the same. The transferring institution must notify the receiving one of the acquisition data (Section 43a(2) sentence 3 EStG). The purchase price and purchase date are carried over, and the holding period continues. According to the case law of the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), a German bank may not charge its own fee for the transfer. It may only pass on third-party costs that it has incurred in the process.

The situation is different if there is a change of creditor (Gläubigerwechsel), that is, if the securities account passes to another person. The transaction is then treated as a sale for the purposes of tax deduction (Section 43(1) sentence 4 EStG). The bank settles as if a sale had taken place, even though no money has changed hands. This fiction only falls away if the person making the transfer expressly informs the bank that it is a transfer free of charge (Section 43(1) sentence 5 EStG). The bank then reports the transaction by 31 May of the following year to the tax office responsible for its place of business (Betriebsstättenfinanzamt), stating the value, the acquisition costs and the details of both parties (Section 43(1) sentence 6 EStG). This report is the normal case and is no disadvantage for the investor. It serves gift tax purposes, and the gift tax allowances are a topic of their own.

bloecke.md:
If the new bank does not have the acquisition data, the tax deduction on a later sale is based on 30% of the sale proceeds (Section 43a(2) sentence 7 EStG). This typically happens with transfers from abroad, from very old securities accounts or from estates. Almost a third of the proceeds is then taxed, regardless of the gain.

For a share position with €10,000 of proceeds and a real gain of €1,000, the bank uses €3,000 as the tax base. This results in €791.25 of tax instead of €263.75. This can only be corrected through the tax return, and the old contract notes are needed for that. Contract notes for securities should therefore be kept permanently, not just for ten years.

## Acquisition costs in the case of a gift

In the case of an acquisition free of charge, the recipient takes over the donor's tax position. The legal predecessor's acquisition and acquisition costs are attributed to the recipient (Section 20(4) sentence 6 EStG). A gift therefore does not reset the entry price. The book gain, and with it the latent tax, passes unchanged to the recipient. Tax-free old holdings remain tax-free, whereas a loss carryforward stays with the donor.

An advantage therefore only arises from the person of the recipient. The recipient has their own saver's allowance and possibly a marginal tax rate below 25%. However, this only works if the gift is genuine. It must be final, nothing may flow back to the donor, and the donor may not in fact continue to control the assets.

Any change in the person of the holder is a change of creditor, including a transfer from a joint securities account to an individual one. Without the express notice that the transfer is free of charge, the bank treats it as a sale.

## Timing of the sale and tax deferral

As long as nothing is sold, the part of the portfolio that economically belongs to the tax office also remains invested and continues to generate returns. This works like an interest-free loan from the state, the value of which grows with the holding period.

An illustrative calculation with €100,000 of starting capital, a gross return of 7% a year and a term of 30 years shows the order of magnitude. In it, realised gains are taxed at 26.375%, there is no partial exemption, and the allowance has been used up. If the sale only takes place at the end, €586,827 remains after tax. With complete reallocation every year, it is €451,588, even though the gross return and the tax rate are the same. The difference of around €135,000 corresponds to 0.9 percentage points of net return a year.

bloecke.md:
Two qualifications apply to this calculation.

First, the advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale) limits the effect for funds. Every year, it taxes a notional minimum return of 70% of the base interest rate (Basiszins), applied to the value at the start of the year (Section 18 InvStG). For 2026, that is 2.24%, because according to the BMF circular of 13 January 2026 the base interest rate is 3.20%. This is the highest value since the rule was introduced. For a portfolio that gains 7% in the same year, around a third of the increase in value is thus taxed in advance, while two thirds remain deferred. Advance lump sums that have been assessed are later deducted in full from the capital gain (Section 19(1) InvStG). The tax on them is therefore an advance payment, not an additional tax.

Second, deferral is not remission. Advertising that promises “saving tax” almost always means “paying tax later”. The advantage lies in the compound interest on the deferred amount, not in the amount itself. It also assumes that the tax rate does not rise before the sale. That depends on future political decisions and cannot be hedged. The current coalition agreement, however, contains no plan to raise or abolish the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer).

The deferral advantage argues against unnecessary reallocation. However, it is no reason to keep a wrong position. A portfolio that is not cleaned up purely for tax reasons continues to carry a cluster risk, and the tax justification does nothing to change that.

Conversely, switching to an ETF that is only slightly cheaper often does not pay off. With a portfolio value of €100,000 and a book gain of €40,000, the switch immediately costs 40,000 × 70% × 26.375% = €7,385 in tax. A cost ratio that is 0.10 percentage points lower, by contrast, brings €100 a year. The tax would admittedly fall due at some point anyway, but it is missing from the invested capital from now on.

- Keep old holdings and new purchases of the same securities in separate securities accounts if a partial sale is foreseeable. The separation must be set up before the purchase.
- Before every partial withdrawal, work out the required number of units from the gain under FIFO, not from the gross amount.
- For every transfer to another person, declare in writing that it is free of charge before the transfer is carried out.
- Keep contract notes and annual tax certificates permanently, especially after changing banks.
- Size unavoidable sales so that the realised gain exactly uses up the saver's allowance.

mitnehmen: A long holding period does not make gains on securities tax-free, but it defers the tax until the sale, and that is where the advantage lies.

Under the mandatory FIFO rule, the oldest units, which usually carry the largest gains, always go first in a partial sale; the only remedy is separate securities accounts, which must already exist before the purchase.
Changing banks without a change of owner does not trigger tax, but if the acquisition data are not passed on, 30% of the proceeds may be used as the tax base.
Every transfer to another person counts as a sale unless it is expressly declared to be free of charge, and this declaration, which costs nothing, saves four-figure sums.
In the 30-year illustrative calculation, around 0.9 percentage points of net return a year depend solely on whether the portfolio is reallocated.

begriffe.text: Abbreviation for “first in, first out”. For securities in collective safe custody, the units bought first are deemed to have been sold first (Section 20(4) sentence 7 EStG). A different allocation by the customer or the bank is irrelevant for tax purposes.
Flat-rate withholding tax not yet due on unrealised price gains. It appears on no securities account statement, but reduces the value that the investor has at their disposal after tax.
Return advantage that arises because tax not yet paid remains invested in the portfolio and earns returns as well. It grows with the holding period. The tax is not waived as a result.

Change in the person of the securities account holder. For the purposes of tax deduction, it counts as a sale unless the transfer is expressly reported as free of charge (Section 43(1) sentences 4 and 5 EStG).
If the bank lacks the acquisition data, it bases the tax deduction on sale on 30% of the proceeds instead of the gain actually made (Section 43a(2) sentence 7 EStG).
